items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Like Claus Ogerman did for Gilberto on the album called “Amaroso.”

ctx.x: Because we are so used to hearing him playing so much piano, that he must have been able to cut back a little bit to accompany the singing. Or how did that work?

Well what he did was he played a lot you know, but he left the melody open so that what he played surrounded you. Like a good arranger would do. Like Claus Ogerman did for Gilberto on the album called “Amaroso.” He didn’t get in Gilberto’s way but if you hear © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -2-

those tunes without the strings, you see what he did. He just filled everything out. And that’s what I did. He knew the melody to everything. So he left that to you to sing it. And everything else he just put there.

items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: That came to me through hearing the João Gilberto version of Desafinado, tracing it down, and finding that there was a whole album of João Gilberto singing Brazilian songs accompanied by and arranged by Antonio Carlos Jobim.

ctx.x: That it is. It’s a remarkable song. The Brazilian recording. How did you come into that? How did that come to you?

That came to me through hearing the João Gilberto version of Desafinado, tracing it down, and finding that there was a whole album of João Gilberto singing Brazilian songs accompanied by and arranged by Antonio Carlos Jobim. I found this album. I was transfixed by this album. I couldn’t – I never stopped playing it. I played it all the time. It was so beautiful to me, and it was so hip. It had all the swing and the creativity of jazz music, and all the excitement, but yet it had the gentleness and the brilliance…
Then when this guy called me to do the lyric to this thing, I thought he was a damned fool.
